Paginate Filters was inspired by Frappe Framework API. This feature is very powerful to support deep search and keep it safe. The format of filter param is a json encoded of multidimensional array.
Maximum array members is three, first index is `column_name`, second index is `operator` and third index is `values`, you can also pass array to values.
You are allowed to send array inside a value.
You can filter nested condition with deep array.

Operator | `string` | `OR` | Default conditional operator if no operator specified. For example `GET /user?filters=[["name","like","jo"],["age",">",20]]`, produces `SELECT * FROM user where name like '%jo' OR age > 20`
FieldWrapper | `string` | `LOWER(%s)` | FieldWrapper for `LIKE` operator *(for postgres default is: `LOWER((%s)::text)`)*
DefaultSize | `int64` | `10` | Default size or limit per page
PageStart | `int64` | `0` | Set start page, default `0` if not set. `total_pages` , `max_page` and `page` variable will be affected if you set `PageStart` greater than `0`

LikeAsIlikeDisabled | `bool` | `false` | By default, paginate using Case Insensitive on `LIKE` operator. Instead of using `ILIKE`, you can use `LIKE` operator to find what you want. You can set `LikeAsIlikeDisabled` to `true` if you need this feature to be disabled.
FieldSelectorEnabled | `bool` | `false` | Enable partial response with specific fields. Comma separated per field. eg: `?fields=title,user.name`

SortParams | `[]string` | `[]string{"sort"}` | if `CustomParamEnabled` is `true`, you can set the `SortParams` with custom parameter names. For example: `[]string{"sorting", "ordering", "other_alternative_param"}`. The following requests will capture same result `?sorting=-name` or `?ordering=-name` or `?other_alternative_param=-name` or `?sort=-name`

PageParams | `[]string` | `[]string{"page"}` | if `CustomParamEnabled` is `true`, you can set the `PageParams` with custom parameter names. For example: `[]string{"number", "num", "other_alternative_param"}`. The following requests will capture same result `?number=0` or `?num=0` or `?other_alternative_param=0` or `?page=0`

SizeParams | `[]string` | `[]string{"size"}` | if `CustomParamEnabled` is `true`, you can set the `SizeParams` with custom parameter names. For example: `[]string{"limit", "max", "other_alternative_param"}`. The following requests will capture same result `?limit=50` or `?limit=50` or `?other_alternative_param=50` or `?max=50`

OrderParams | `[]string` | `[]string{"order"}` | if `CustomParamEnabled` is `true`, you can set the `OrderParams` with custom parameter names. For example: `[]string{"order", "direction", "other_alternative_param"}`. The following requests will capture same result `?order=desc` or `?direction=desc` or `?other_alternative_param=desc`

FilterParams | `[]string` | `[]string{"filters"}` | if `CustomParamEnabled` is `true`, you can set the `FilterParams` with custom parameter names. For example: `[]string{"search", "find", "other_alternative_param"}`. The following requests will capture same result `?search=["name","john"]` or `?find=["name","john"]` or `?other_alternative_param=["name","john"]` or `?filters=["name","john"]`

|`docker-compose.prod.yml`|Production overrides (external proxy network, no exposed ports)|
|`all`|postgres, redis, mqtt, observer, migrate, collector, api, web|Everything on one host|
|`core`|postgres, redis (dev override only), migrate, collector, api, web|Central server infrastructure|
|`observer`|packet capture observer|Observes RF traffic and publishes to MQTT|

**Note:** Most deployments connect to an external MQTT broker. Add `--profile mqtt` only if you need a local broker. The `observer` profile runs meshcore-packet-capture to observe MeshCore RF traffic and publish decoded packets to MQTT.

**Database note:** the bundled `postgres` container joins the `core` profile only when using `docker-compose.dev.yml` (profiles merge across override files), so the zero-config dev workflow is unchanged. Production (`docker-compose.prod.yml`) deliberately leaves it out — the bundled container's `postgres` network alias would shadow a shared instance of the same name on the same Docker network. Point the `DATABASE_*` variables at your shared/external instance, or opt in explicitly with `--profile postgres` / `--profile all`. See docs/database.md.

One graph across all languages, with cross-service HTTP/gRPC/queue edges and architecture gates with ratchet baselines. Not a security dataflow engine.|

|**Joern**|Open-source Code Property Graph for vulnerability research, queried with a Scala DSL.|Architecture-level ontology instead of a low-level CPG, standard OpenCypher, and MCP / VS Code / CI integration out of the box.|

|**Serena** and other LSP-based MCP servers|Precise symbol lookup and editing for agents through language servers.|Gives agents the system view (cross-service calls, data lineage, blast radius) rather than symbol-level edits. Works well alongside an LSP-based server.|

|**`codebase-memory-mcp` (`CBM`)**|Fast Go/C Tree-sitter structural & call-graph indexing (`96.9s` on `twenty`), low RAM usage, branch graph diffing (`compare_graphs`), and runtime trace overlays (`ingest_traces`).|Adds Layer 4–5 architectural ontology (ORM/SQL database tables, `READS_FROM`/`WRITES_TO` lineage, BullMQ/Kafka queues, GraphQL/REST endpoints), NestJS DI call resolution, and CI Semantic Invariant Gates (Case Study 03).|

|**`graphify`**|Unsupervised Leiden community clustering, cross-community bridge detection (`graphify://surprises`), docstring rationale extraction, GitHub PR triage, and Obsidian/HTML knowledge vault exports.|Scales to 24.5k-file monorepos (`147s` vs. `>45m` timeout on `twenty`), queries an indexed SQLite database via OpenCypher (`599ms` cold MCP init vs. `3.7s`), and models endpoints, queues, and database lineage (Case Study 04).|

|**ArchUnit**, **NetArchTest**, **dependency-cruiser**|Architecture rules written as tests inside one language ecosystem. ArchUnit can also freeze existing violations.|One rule language (OpenCypher) across languages and services, and the same graph also powers visualization and agent context.|

The question that interested me was how MPs' positions develop over time. Answering it means connecting what someone said in one debate with their contributions years later, even as their constituency or the way their name is printed changes. Parliament's SPRS publishes the reports, but those connections take work to put together:
The older debates are surprisingly fun to read, too. One of my favourite finds is Tan Cheng Tong's 1963 exchange, where the original insult seems to survive only through the outrage it provoked.
- Find your MP by choosing a constituency on the people page, starting with the latest Parliament.
- A person's page brings together the Parliaments they sat in, their attendance and their contributions, with links to the reports they contributed to.

- A report groups the text into speeches, with links to speakers where they've been identified. The transcript keeps its original spelling, even when a misspelt speaker label links to the right person.
- A speech link takes you straight to a contribution. Copy link, Cite and Report an error sit on each paragraph so you can share it, quote it or flag a problem where you found it.
- A sitting puts the day's reports beside its lists of members present and absent.
- Search lets you follow a subject through speeches and report titles, then narrow it by Parliament, date, report type, person or constituency.

I opened the site to the public on 20 October 2026. It is an unofficial project, and the Official Report on SPRS remains the authoritative record. Each report links back there so readers can check my work against the source.
The records come from my separate hansard-scraper project. The coverage page tracks what's available, while the methods explain how I build the connections and where gaps remain.

The site is non-partisan on purpose. It sorts the record so you can browse it, and it publishes no analysis of its own, such as comparisons between parties, rankings of members, or a verdict on how a member's views changed. The site's colour scheme avoids party colours for the same reason. The scraper's vision sets out where that line sits.

If you find something wrong, email me at contact@openhansard.sg. The "Report an error" action on each paragraph fills in its speech's address for you, which helps me find the passage you mean. If you prefer to report it publicly, use the Report an error form.

I'm Royce Hoe, and I build and maintain the site on my own. When the archive introduces an error in the text or credits the wrong speaker, I fix it and record the change in the corrections log. If Parliament asks me to take down a report, I do so within 2 working days, without asking for a reason.

I used AI coding tools for most of the implementation and documented the process, my decisions and the audits in How this was built. The documentation index brings together the design decisions, data notes and guides for anyone who wants to look further.

I want to see where the site makes sense to someone else and where it gets in their way. The user-testing protocol sets out five tasks, from finding and sharing a speech to checking a citation and reporting an error. No sessions have run yet; that page is where I'll record what people get stuck on and what I change as a result.

**Automatic pre-migration snapshot (SQLite).** Whenever a SQLite-backed instance has pending migrations to apply, Pad first copies the database file to `pad.db.pre-<version>-m<migration>` next to it, where `<migration>` is the number of the newest migration the binary ships, so each upgrade that adds migrations gets its own snapshot. If an upgrade ever goes wrong, stop the server and copy that snapshot back over `pad.db`. After a successful upgrade, Pad keeps that upgrade's snapshot and the newest earlier one, and removes older `pad.db.pre-<version>-m<migration>` files it created. It never removes a file with any other name (a copy you made by hand, an older `pad.db.pre-<version>` snapshot); those are left for you to delete. This is a convenience net, not a backup strategy — keep your own backups (see docs/backup.md). PostgreSQL instances are skipped here; use `pg_dump` or a provider snapshot before upgrading.

Next, what happens inside one tool call, in How it works.

One tool call, step by step: the agent runs a tool, the PreToolUse hook denies a big Read and names the ctx_execute call, the MCP server runs it in the sandbox, SQLite FTS5 keeps the output, and after compaction a state block of at most 2,048 B comes back.

1. **Install.** Each agent's own install command adds the MCP server, the hooks and the skills `ctx-doctor`, `ctx-stats` and `ctx-upgrade` to that agent's config folder, for example `~/.codex/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`. `context-mode setup` writes or repairs any part the native command leaves out (ADR-0023).
2. **Session start.** The `SessionStart` hook opens the project database. When the session ran before, the agent gets one line that tells it to call `ctx_resume` (dispatch.ts).

3. **PreToolUse checks.** Before a tool runs, the `PreToolUse` hook checks the call in a fixed order: the user's deny list, WebFetch, curl and wget, inline HTTP and build commands, then a full-file Read over `OUTPUT_CAP` (16,384 B) and one-file shell dumps such as `cat` or `tail`. A Read with a line range runs as usual (decide.ts).

4. **The exact call.** When a check matches, the hook stops the call and its reply names the exact `ctx_*` call to use, for example `ctx_execute` with `{"language":"shell","code":"<the command>","intent":"<what you need>"}`. For WebFetch the reply names `ctx_index`, then `ctx_search` (read-deny.ts).

5. **The sandbox.** This is the Code Mode step: the agent's script runs here, and only what it prints comes back. `ctx_execute` writes the script to a temp folder and spawns the runtime from an argument list in the project folder. The timeout is `EXEC_TIMEOUT_MS` (600,000 ms, default and maximum); on timeout it stops the whole process group (`taskkill /F /T` on Windows). The child gets your environment minus preload variables such as `NODE_OPTIONS`, and the agent gets what the script prints, at most `OUTPUT_CAP` (execute.ts).

**Code Mode.** The agent sends a short script as a tool parameter, the script reads the data in the sandbox, and only what it prints goes into the context. Two real calls, in the form the Claude Code terminal shows them:
`ctx_execute` on 5,000 JSON records, from the Claude Code 2.1.312 stream of the Try-it run with Context Mode 2.0.0-next.26 (04-api-json.json). The data is 1,039,898 B; the agent gets 254 B.

`ctx_batch` on an install log and a long git log, one live MCP call to `release-out/server.mjs` of Context Mode 2.0.0-next.36 on 2026-11-03 (2026-11-03-ctx-batch.json). The commands print 228,881 B; the agent gets 8,667 B, the parts that match its two queries, and the full output stays in the index.

6. **Indexing.** The full output goes into the index in chunks of at most `MAX_CHUNK_BYTES` (4,096 B). A Markdown chunk stays inside one heading section, and a code block that fits stays whole. Each chunk goes into two SQLite FTS5 tables: a Porter-stemmed table for words and a trigram table for paths, names and parts of words (fts.ts).

`ctx_index` on a copy of this repo's `docs/how-it-works.md`, one live MCP call to `release-out/server.mjs` of Context Mode 2.0.0-next.36 on 2026-11-03 (calls.json). The file is 11,577 B; the agent gets 64 B.

7. **Search.** `ctx_search` ranks each table with BM25 and joins the two lists with Reciprocal Rank Fusion: a hit scores 1/(`RRF_K` + rank), with `RRF_K` = 60. Before it returns an empty list, it tries a spelling fix from the indexed words. Search covers this session, this worktree (the default) or the whole project, and each snippet is at most `SNIPPET_MAX_BYTES` (800 B) (search.ts).

`ctx_search` on that index, in the same run, in a project that also holds an `AGENTS.md`. One search reads the index and every agent's memory files. The agent gets 1,268 B: one content hit and one memory hit, each with its source and heading. For memory shared across machines, agents and sessions, see Context Mode Gateway Memory.

8. **Run, then replace.** On hosts that run the tool first, the `PostToolUse` hook checks the result. Output over `REPLACE_TRIGGER_BYTES` (4,096 B) goes into the index whole, and the agent gets the best-matching chunks and one `ctx_search` line for the rest (dispatch.ts).

9. **Journal and compaction.** The hooks log each prompt, edit, command, tool error and decision in a journal. After a compaction the agent gets a state block of at most `STATE_BUDGET` (2,048 B), and each long line becomes a `ctx_resume(seq)` pointer to the full row; one `ctx_resume` reply is at most `RESUME_CAP` (2,048 B). On the next prompt, a prompt-match block brings back the journal rows that match it by BM25 (ADR-0009).
`ctx_resume` with empty parameters returns the state block, in the same run: 209 B.

10. **The database.** Each project has one `context.db` under `~/.context-mode`, in Node's built-in `node:sqlite`. The database runs in WAL mode and runs a PASSIVE checkpoint on close. A new database gets built under a temp name and moves into place in one atomic step, and the busy timeout is `DB_TIMEOUT_MS` (5,000 ms) (db.ts).

11. **A hook error.** A hook always ends with exit 0. On any error it gives the host's allow reply and writes one log line to `~/.context-mode/hook-errors.log`, so your agent keeps working. A spawned hook has `HOOK_TIMEOUT_MS` (5,000 ms) (fallback.ts).
